Lesson overview:
- Level: A0 General English
- Unit: Unit 2. Big happy family
- Time: 60 min (Essential) / 90 min (Expanded) / 120 min (Full Workshop)
- Focus: How do you feel today?
- Materials: Feeling face cards, emoji cards, whiteboard, COSYmanuals 'to be' and 'adjectives' pages.
By the end of this lesson, you can:

• express feelings and emotions using 'to be' + adjective
• ask partners about their current emotional state

Quick retrieval task: which words or phrases do you remember?
Which word belongs to the previous lesson?
Core Active Vocabulary (10 items):

fine — well or okay. Example: I am fine, thank you.
happy — feeling good and positive. Example: I am happy today.
sad — feeling unhappy. Example: He is sad because it is raining.
tired — needing rest. Example: I am tired after work.
good — fine or positive. Example: The food is good.
hungry — wanting to eat. Example: I am hungry at noon.
thirsty — wanting to drink. Example: She is thirsty after sport.
excited — very happy about something. Example: We are excited about the holiday.
bored — not interested. Example: The children are bored.
worried — feeling nervous about a problem. Example: She is worried about the exam.
Essential Chunks & Functional Collocations:

• How do you feel today? (asking about feelings)
• I am happy. (positive feeling)
• I am tired. (negative feeling)
• Are you okay? (checking on someone)
• I am not sad. (negative sentence about feelings)
• What's wrong? (asking about a problem)
Vocabulary practice: choose the correct word.
Which word means 'well or okay'?
Which word means 'feeling good and positive'?
Complete the sentence with a word from the list.
Pronunciation Focus: Adjective endings and intonation in feeling questions

happy /ˈhæpi/ — stress the first syllable
tired /ˈtaɪəd/ — two syllables
excited /ɪkˈsaɪtɪd/ — stress the second syllable
worried /ˈwʌrid/ — stress the first syllable

How do you feel today? I am happy. Are you tired?

elements.content: Grammar Focus: Use 'be' to say who someone is, how they feel, and where they are from.

Form:
The verb 'to be': I am / You are / He, she, it is / We are / They are. Negative: I'm not, isn't, aren't. Question: Am I...? Are you...? Is he...?

Examples:
• I am a student.
• She is from Spain.
• We are happy today.
• They are not teachers.
Controlled practice: choose the correct form.
My name ___ Alex.
They ___ from Italy.
I ___ tired today.
She ___ not a teacher.
Substitution drill: say the sentence with the new words.

• I am ... (a student / happy / from Egypt).
• She is ... (a teacher / tired / from Spain).
• They are ... (students / at home / happy).
Question-answer practice: ask and answer with your partner.

• Are you a student? — Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
• Is she from France? — Yes, she is. / No, she isn't.
• Are they happy? — Yes, they are. / No, they aren't.
Personalised production: use the structure about your own life.

• Write two true sentences with 'I am...' and 'I am not...'.
• Introduce two people in the class with 'He/She is...'.
Reading: How do you feel today?

How do you feel today? I am happy and fine. My brother is tired after work. My sister is excited about her birthday. My mother is hungry and my father is thirsty. Our dog is bored at home. We are not sad today. We are all good.
How does the brother feel?
Who is excited?
Listening: listen to the dialogue and answer the questions.

A: Hi, Sara. How do you feel today?
B: I'm fine, thanks. A little tired.
A: Are you okay?
B: Yes, I'm okay. I'm just hungry.
A: Me too! Let's have lunch.
B: Great idea. I'm excited about our English class later.
How does Sara feel at first?
Why is Sara hungry?
Speaking task: Ask your partner how they feel today and why. Ask about two family members too.

• How do you feel today?
• What makes you happy?
• What makes you tired?
• Are you usually hungry in the morning?
• How do you help a friend who is sad?
Role-play: You meet a friend after school. Ask how they feel, listen to the answer, and respond with a helpful suggestion.
Work in pairs. Take turns. Use at least five target words and one target grammar structure. Then swap roles.
Writing task: Write five sentences about how you and your family feel today.
Model: I am ... My mother is ... My father is ... My brother is ... We are ...
